Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid People: avoid other people, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person

Vignette:
Rohan was seven when his stepfather’s temper began to shape the geography of his home. The punishments arrived without warning. He remembered the heavy oak door at the end of the hallway, how it would swing shut with a concussive slam that vibrated through the floorboards. He also remembered the unheated cellar, a damp space where he was left for hours. It was not just the dark that made him shiver, but the exact, biting temperature of the concrete floor and the iron pipes—a specific, metallic chill that seeped into his forearms until his teeth ached. Rohan survived by memorizing the rhythm of that latch and waiting for the heavy thud of footsteps to pass. Decades later, at thirty-six, a detective with the county police department, Rohan found his life fracturing around those same sensations. At work, the precinct’s heavy doors swinging shut behind witnesses triggered a reflexive startle that left his pen shaking. In the breakroom, when a colleague’s hand brushed his shoulder, leaving the lingering cold of a refrigerated coffee machine on his sleeve, Rohan’s chest tightened. It was not the touch, but that precise temperature on his skin that sent a jolt through him. Rohan had come to believe that his body was still waiting in that cellar, bracing for the slam. Over the past two years, cautious adjustments hardened into rigid routines. Rohan began delaying sleep, staying awake in the kitchen until the house settled, terrified of drifting off alone. Closing his eyes in his marital bed felt like surrendering to a silence he could not monitor. Rohan told himself he was catching up on reports, though the reality was simpler: he avoided going out to certain neighborhoods, taking back routes to the station even when it cost him hours. He stopped answering calls from old friends, building a quiet distance to keep anyone from seeing how easily he fractured. His wife noticed the pullback, the way Rohan flinched when their bedroom door clicked shut, the way he stopped sharing his days with her because he could no longer bear the prospect of sleeping alone. The weight of these habits accumulated steadily. At the precinct, Rohan volunteered for desk assignments to avoid door-to-door canvasses, knowing the street level brought him too close to sudden movements and echoing stairwells. The cold of a November patrol car seat, the slam of the evidence room door, and the stillness of his own apartment all existed side by side in his days. Through it all, Rohan held onto a quiet conviction that there was something wrong with him as a person. He felt like he did not know himself anymore, that the steady officer his wife had married had been replaced by someone who constantly monitored exits and flinched at drafts. Rohan had come to believe that his reactions since the event showed he was a lousy coper. The breaking point arrived quietly during a Tuesday shift, when a station door swung open behind him and Rohan found himself unable to sit still, his breath short, his hands gripping his desk until his knuckles whitened. He realized he could no longer outpace the past. Rohan had scheduled an appointment with a trauma specialist, not because he believed he would be fixed, but because the exhaustion of his own avoidance had finally outweighed his fear. He hoped someone might help him understand why a specific chill or a closing door still felt like a threat. What frightened Rohan most was that he would never stop bracing for the slam, that he would spend the rest of his life waiting for permission to feel safe.
